newsitem.title: UK: Russia faces severe fiscal challenge -S&P.
newsitem.headline: Russia faces severe fiscal challenge -S&P.

text.p: Russia faces a severe fiscal challenge, Standard & Poor's Corp said on Tuesday.

"There are severe fiscal challenges that face the (Russian) government, and the question to ask is whether there has been a fundamental and radical change there," David Beers, managing director for sovereign ratings group at S&P told Reuters.
Beers declined to comment on whether Russia would be upgraded during S&P's annual review later this year.

"In fact, the fiscal situation worsened after the rating (was assigned), although the new government is now better placed to deal with the situation and has clawed back some of the deterioration," Beers said.
Last October, S&P assigned Russia's long-term foreign currency debt a BB minus rating, with a stable outlook. Moody's Investors Service gave Russia a Ba2 rating.
Neither is investment grade, but both were better than expected at the time.
Beers said S&P outlook attached to the rating indicated what it expected the rating to be for the next one to three years.

London-based analysts on Monday said Russia's chances of getting a sovereign credit upgrade this year were slim, although economic and fiscal improvements could lead to a change in the outlook to positive from stable.

When S&P rated Russia's debt in October of last year, it said the key factors constraining the rating were the government's short economic management track record and, especially, the difficulties it faced in raising tax revenues; the challenge of leadership in a country with a still developing democratic culture and political institutions and a weak legal system.
Russian President Boris Yeltsin installed a new reformist cabinet in March, and since then pension arrears have been paid and inflation and interest rates have come down.
Among problems still facing Russia are unpaid bills between companies and the state, which nearly doubled to 27 percent of gross domestic product over the first half of the year.
In October Russia will put the budget and revisions to the budget before the Duma (parliament), and analysts said progress there would be key in determining its rating outlook.
Since receiving its ratings, Russia has tapped the Eurobond market and become a benchmark for the region.
In November it launched a $1.0 billion five-year bond. In March, Russia issued a 2.0 billion mark seven-year bond. In June, it borrowed $2.0 billion at 10 years.
Bankers said the doubling of both size and maturity in the dollar bond market in such a short period of time indicated improved investor sentiment towards the country.
